Title: InQuest Game picks V:TES as all-time best multi-player CCG

Messages.Author: LSJ
Messages.Body:
FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE

Direct Inquiries to:
Philippe Boulle, Marketing Director
White Wolf Publishing
1554 Litton Drive
Stone Mountain, GA 30083
prbo...@white-wolf.com
404-292-1819 x203

INQUEST GAMER picks VAMPIRE: THE ETERNAL STRUGGLE®
as all-time best multiplayer CCG

Atlanta, GA, January 30, 2004 - InQuest Gamer, an industry-leading
magazine, has named White Wolf's Vampire: The Eternal Struggle as the
best multiplayer collectible card game of all time.

The article, appearing in the March 2004 issue of InQuest Gamer (#107),
examines all the top collectible card games based on their play in games
with more than two players, examining (among others) the variety of
viable strategies in multiplayer games and how much interaction went on
between players. Vampire: The Eternal Struggle (or VTES) soared to the
top of the list, eclipsing such well-known games as Lord of the Rings
and Magic: The Gathering. "[VTES] combines the best of one-on-one play
with multiplayer while remaining balanced," said InQuest, and paid
special attention to importance of diplomacy and politics in the game.
"The politics of the setting shine through in the CCG... Diplomacy isn't
just an aspect of [VTES], it's a necessity."

"Right after he designed the world's best dueling CCG in Magic: The
Gathering, Richard Garfield designed the world's best multiplayer CCG in
Vampire: The Eternal Struggle. CCG fans who haven't experienced real
multiplayer CCG strategy owe it to themselves to pick up some Vampire
starters and see why InQuest rated it number one," said Steve Wieck,
White Wolf's director of card development. L. Scott Johnson, line
developer for VTES, added, "The game emphasizes making (and the threat
of breaking) deals so that it doesn't feel like each player is just
playing solitaire. But the predator/prey constraints and victory
conditions ensure that the deal-making aspect doesn't overshadow deck
building and card play."

Vampire: The Eternal Struggle is a collectible card game based on White
Wolf's award-winning roleplaying game, Vampire: The Masquerade. In VTES,
players take on the roll of ancient vampires called Methuselahs who use
a variety of vampiric agents (represented by cards) to act against one
another. These actions (also represented by cards) can be aimed at
physical resources, political influence or even social spheres. Unlike
many other such card games, VTES is designed primarily for multiple
players, and its official tournaments use that format (rather than the
one-on-one duels more common in other games). First introduced in 1994,
VTES celebrates its tenth anniversary this year and is going stronger
than ever, with more organized play than ever before. VTES's next
set "Vampire: The Eternal Struggle - Gehenna" releases this May.

(Vampire: The Eternal Struggle - Gehenna 36-pack booster display: WW02651;
$99.00; Individual 11-card booster pack: $2.75 MSRP)

More information about VTES is available at
http://www.white-wolf.com/vtes/ .

Since its entry into the roleplaying game market in 1991, White Wolf
Publishing, Inc. has grown, maintaining an average market share of 26%.
With collective book sales in excess of 5.5 million copies during this
time, White Wolf is one of two undisputed worldwide publishing leaders
for pen and paper roleplaying games. White Wolf properties have been
licensed for television series, comic books, action figures, console and
computer video games, coin-operated arcade games, professional
wrestlers, replica props and weapons, interactive media events, and a
myriad of merchandise. More information on White Wolf can be found at
www.white-wolf.com .

InQuest Gamer is a publication of Wizard Entertainment, based in
Congers, New York. launched in 1997, InQuest Gamer has proven to be the
ultimate source for information about collectible card games,
roleplaying games, and all fantasy gaming. More information on InQuest
Gamer can be found at www.wizarduniverse.com .

Vampire and Vampire the Eternal Struggle are registered trademarks of
White Wolf Publishing. Gehenna is a trademark of White Wolf Publishing.
All rights reserved.

Messages.Author: Curevei
Messages.Body:
While I would agree with IQ in this regard, I just received my copy for issue
106 wherein they rate all English CCGs. I find their ratings rather useless,
showing about as much bias as can be expected of any group of people who play a
variety of CCGs.

Wheel of Time as a hall of fame game? As much enjoyment I gained from being
involved with it, let's say that I had a hard time selling large numbers of
people on a two-player CCG that often took us 2 hours to play (with shortcuts)
and eventually required rolling 100s of dice ... in a single turn.

On the flip side, Shadowfist escapes their hall of fame designation? I might
not personally like playing the game as I don't like easy removal and easy
comebacks, but I'm willing to consider it the only multiplayer CCG in V:TES's
league.

Maybe they give some sort of objective criteria for how they rank games in
issue 107, but as is, it just seems to me that it comes down to "I like game X
more than game Y", which is fine if all you want to do is market the games you
like. I found Scrye's ratings, which are broken down into categories, found in
their guide to CCGs, a lot more plausible, with the added benefit of more in
depth descriptions of what the game's about and, maybe, why they ended up with
some of their ratings.

Well, ranting aside, it does help market V:TES, which is good. And, it has no
effect on my favorite CCG (which they think sucks) as it died long ago.

Messages.Author: The Fanboy
Messages.Body:
> Was it in substance a VTES-type game with only the fight options, was there
> real strategy of deckbuilding and playing etc ?

No. It was developed seperately from VTEs entirely (WoTC developed
VTES, WW developed Rage). Play style is completely different.

Game play begins with all your Garou in play, up to a maximum renown
value determined before play begins. Each player picks their alpha
(acting minion for the turn).

Then everyone just drops non-combat cards on the table. Literally.
Everything happens at once.

Then one person challenges another and combat begins. Strikes are
committed to before exposed, so you can't respond to your opponents
strike.

Games are short and bloody. Timing issues abound because everything
happens at once. There is politics (called Moots), but most people
don't play with them. VPs are based on what renown value of Garou and
monsters you kill.

Players who make combat decks and achieve personal victory in VTES by
torporing/burning vampires and could care less about ousting would
LOVE Rage.

A few years later, 5RP released a revised version that had more
concrete timing rules and slower play. The revised game tanked
(partly because it looked identical to the old game, but lots of rules
changed and many cards changed effects -- moreso than any errata we've
seen in VTES).

Fanboy

Messages.Author: Andrew S. Davidson
Messages.Body:
On 30 Jan 2004 21:51:24 GMT, Curevei wrote:

>On the flip side, Shadowfist escapes their hall of fame designation? I might
>not personally like playing the game as I don't like easy removal and easy
>comebacks, but I'm willing to consider it the only multiplayer CCG in V:TES's
>league.

I haven't read the March Inquest article yet but amused by the
comments from Steve Wieck and LSJ about deal-making. This feature of
real-world VTES play make it inferior to Shadowfist, IMO. And what's
odd is that it's not an overt part of the game mechanics. Neither the
Shadowfist rules nor the VTES rules say anything to suggest that you
make deals or alliances. That these don't tend to happen in one game
but do tend to happen in the other is quite subtle.

That aside, I'm sure that Shadowfist is the better multi-player game
because it's hard to eliminate players during the course of the game
and it's feasible to come back from a weakened position to win. It's
no fun to be ousted and yet that's what VTES is all about.

The main difficulty with a multi-player game is finding all those
other players to play with. VTES scores well in that respect because
it got good market penetration, being the first CCG to appear after
Magic. Magic is still popular, not because it is a particularly good
CCG (it was as we know quite broken) but because it was first. VTES
was the first multiplayer CCG and, even though it was quite broken
too, also rests upon this advantage.

At our games club in Finchley, the two multiplayer CCGs which are
currently played are Shadowfist and Game of Thrones. The latter must
have its merits but I'm still not going to try it - the theme doesn't
interest me. That's the strength of VTES for me - its theme. I
really must break open those unopened boxes of Rage I have and see if
the similar WoD theme works better there. There are just too many of
these games. Anyone tried Cyberpunk yet ...?

Andrew

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
Andrew S. Davidson wrote:

> That these don't tend to happen in one game
> but do tend to happen in the other is quite subtle.

It doesn't really strike me as that subtle.

In Shadowfist, there is nothing at all to gain by helping someone else
win--no VPs, only "Game Winer" and "Losers". There isn't really any half
measure winner in Shadowfist, so the incentive to make a deal to help
someone win isn't really there. It is possible that the current tournament
rules have some sort of well defined second/third/forth place that I haven't
seen yet, but from what I understand, there was nothing but winning and tie
breaker points.

In VTES there is defenite incentive to make deals--portioned out VPs. Often,
making a deal for 2 VPs to help someone get 3 VPs 'cause you are in a bad
position is the best you can hope for, and thus the deal makes perfect sense
(in a Machiavellian sense), epsecially as VPs are often very significant in
getting into the final round.

In Shadowfist, on the other hand, there is a lot of incentive to form
temporary alliances and make temporary deals to cut the winner back (just
the other day, I convinced an opponent to Golden Comback someone so I could
get back my Underworld Tracker, and we could both team up to stop someone
else from making a winning move--a deal/alliance is made. But it was over as
soon as I could make my own win attempt). But because of the structure of
the game--only 1 winner, and no clear cut way to determine 2nd/3rd/4th
place--making "king maker" deals isn't really an attractive option.

as directly as you describe in our games. Sometimes it does, but it's much
more common for one of us to figure out a way to puncture the game's
equilibrium. Hitting a strong player's site with an Orbital Laser Strike so
that the next player has an incentive to attack it, or using Tortured
Memories/Vivisector to get rid of a big hitter...there are dozens of ways to
do this.

And if you're in the second seat, you have to ask yourself, am I being set
up? Is the guy on my right going to be able to surge for the win once he's
gotten me to wear myself out doing his dirty work for him? Or is there
something I know that he doesn't?

Another dynamic I see a lot is one where someone has built a really powerful
engine into his deck. Sure, he only has one site in play and one BFV, but
he's got three Simian Liberation Armies in his smoked pile, four Simian
Sneakers came back into play when his last site got seized, he's got a SAM
Simian out and he's playing with Diamond Beach, he just dropped two Claw Of
Furies when someone Scrounged him for characters, there's an Inauspicious
Return in his smoked pile, and he's got an Orange Sage in play. This guy's
a threat *now*, because when he makes his big push for victory it's going to
be a *big* push -- in fact, it may already be too late to beat this guy.
(Unless there's a Dragon player in the game. Heh.)

In games like this one, the dynamic is not so much about beating on the guy
who's pushing for the win, it's trying to figure out how to throw sand in
his engine's gears. (The flaw with playing decks like this is that your
cards are, literally, out on the table, which is why in our group people who
play like this have a lot of fun but don't win much.) Or to take advantage
of it. (In this game, I happened to be playing a Shaolin Agent deck, which
loves weenie decks.)

I think the build-up-and-go dynamic you describe is certainly part of the
game, but I also think there's a lot more to it than it sounds like.

Bob Rossney
r...@well.com

>In Shadowfist, there is nothing at all to gain by helping someone else

>

>(in a Machiavellian sense), epsecially as VPs are often very significant in

>

>the game--only 1 winner, and no clear cut way to determine 2nd/3rd/4th
>place--making "king maker" deals isn't really an attractive option.

This probably makes sense, but it would make a lot more sense to me to fail to
see enduring alliances if I didn't play another multiplayer CCG that also had
poorly defined "not first places". I've discussed the differences in play
style between 'fist and V:TES and I still wonder why you don't get two players
who decide to not screw with each other and basically fight it out between
themselves for first/second. Is it just that this doesn't work as the
non-cooperating opponents will just throw the game to one member of the

>I haven't read the March Inquest article yet but amused by the

I don't have any problem with being ousted. The situation that sucks IMO with
V:TES is playing while having no chance of winning, which is why I don't like
rush decks, wall decks, Brainwash, Sens. Dep., milling, etc.

Even if being ousted is unpleasant, there are benefits to such a mechanic. As
players drop, kingmaking ability drops. Speeds play up. OTOH, I'm sure there
are table politics issues with the threat of taking yourself out of games that
are problematic.

>The main difficulty with a multi-player game is finding all those
>other players to play with. VTES scores well in that respect because
>it got good market penetration, being the first CCG to appear after
>Magic. Magic is still popular, not because it is a particularly good
>CCG (it was as we know quite broken) but because it was first. VTES
>was the first multiplayer CCG and, even though it was quite broken

Magic has a lot of advantages besides being first. V:TES has decent market
penetration because the WoD is so well known amongst gamers and because Jyhad
boxes went for so little for so long. Not to say it doesn't have an advantage
in age, but I think it gets a lot less "first on the block" advantage than
Magic does.

I only hear about Cyberpunk secondhand, and I know secondhand info can be wrong
as well as biased, so I'll pass.

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
Curevei wrote:

> This probably makes sense, but it would make a lot more sense to me to fail to
> see enduring alliances if I didn't play another multiplayer CCG that also had
> poorly defined "not first places". I've discussed the differences in play
> style between 'fist and V:TES and I still wonder why you don't get two players
> who decide to not screw with each other and basically fight it out between
> themselves for first/second.

'Cause in Shadowfist, there really isn't a second place. The victory
conditions are "Get to 5 Feng Shui sites, stealing the 5th". There aren't
victory points, really, and having 4 Feng Shui sites when someone wins
doesn't really mean that you are in second place to any meaningful extent.
There have been countless ranking systems in Fist for figuring out what
place you get in a given tournament game, for tie breaker purposes (such as
"Count Feng Shui sites in play at end of game" or "Count Feng Shui Stites
burned for victory" at the end of the game. Or something.), but really, none
of them are that significant, in terms of actually determining a "place".
Having 5 Feng Shui sites means you win. Having 4 means very little--you
could easily have 4 Feng Shui sites in play on the 4th turn simply by
playing one per turn, but then you likely don't have any resources or
characters or any remote chance of winning. In VTES, victory points are a
solid indicator of success in a given game--if one guy has 3 and another has
2, the guy with 2 clearly did well enough to justify having second place. In
Fist, that really isn't the case, such that fighting for second place isn't
worth doing, and being in second place doesn't really mean anything.

> Is it just that this doesn't work as the
> non-cooperating opponents will just throw the game to one member of the
> alliance and end the game?

Throwing the game just to make it end is always a possibility, but that is
either just dumb (and doesn't get you anywhere) or collusion (and as such,
cheating).

This last year at Origins, there was a legendary game (in the land of Fist
geekiness) that went on for an *absurdly* long time--I think the single, 4
player game, went on for 9 hours. Primarily, 'cause it was very balanced,
and no one wanted to accidentally make someone else win, and there was zero
incentive to make a deal to help someone else win, as second place doesn't
really mean anything. This being said, this is a *very* extreme example, and
most games don't do this.
